name: Artificial hair integrations

lead: Artificial hair integrations blend human or synthetic hair into your own to add length, volume and coverage, and to camouflage hair loss from conditions such as alopecia. The fuller look is there as soon as they are applied.
Added hair is clipped, bonded, sewn, fused or pulled through a mesh base so it merges with existing hair. Attachment methods include tape-in, clip-in, micro rings, fusion, weaving and wigs.

paras: They are non-surgical and reversible, used for styling and for hair-loss coverage. Synthetic fibre such as Kanekalon costs much less than human hair but wears out faster under heat and friction. No clinical trials were found.
Prolonged tension, such as tight braiding, can cause traction alopecia, and adhesives are linked to skin reactions, dermatitis and headaches.

angle.text: Users with thinning hair or alopecia use weaves, hairpieces and integration systems to add length, volume and coverage right away. Added hair is attached to their own so thin areas are covered; traction and adhesive issues are documented separately.

lead: Artificial hair integrations are prosthetic hair products, such as extensions, weaves, hairpieces and mesh-based integration systems, that add length, volume or coverage to a person's own hair using human or synthetic fibre. People use them to look like they have a fuller head of hair straight away: restoring a lower hairline or denser crown after thinning, adding length, or changing style without waiting for hair to grow.[1][2][3]

Wikipedia lists attachment methods including tape-in, clip-in, micro rings, fusion, weaving and wigs, and notes that synthetic fibre such as Kanekalon costs much less than human hair but wears out faster under heat and friction.[2] Integration systems pull the wearer's own hair through a perforated mesh base so the added strands blend with it.[1][3]

A dermatology review of hair camouflage lists wigs, extensions, concealing powders and sprays, scalp tattoos and transplants as the options available to people who want to conceal hair loss, and notes that hair loss can affect many parts of a person's life.[4] On looksmax.org the idea is discussed as a route to a younger-looking hairline for men with receding hair, alongside questions about how detectable it is.[5] Reported risks include traction alopecia, skin reactions to adhesives and allergens in synthetic fibre.[2][6][7]
infobox: Human hair or synthetic fibre such as Kanekalon[2]
Clip, tape, bond, sew, thread, mesh[2]

paras: Human hair is sourced largely from Vietnam, India and China, with India, Singapore and Pakistan the largest exporters according to Wikipedia.[2] Synthetic options use fibres such as Kanekalon, and Futura is a more heat-tolerant polyester that cannot be coloured.[2] Integration systems pull natural hair through a perforated mesh base to blend with added strands, and Grokipedia describes human-hair products lasting two to three years with care, while synthetic ones last months to about a year.[1]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, dates artificial hairpieces to ancient Egypt around 3400 BC.[1] Wikipedia reports that wigs were fashionable in the late 17th century, that weaves appeared among celebrities in the 1950s and spread in the 1970s, and that Kanekalon was developed by Kaneka in the 1950s.[2]

Wigs and extensions are worn by people with alopecia totalis and by people experiencing hair loss from treatments such as chemotherapy.[2] A review in the International Journal of Women's Dermatology describes camouflage as including wigs, extensions, powders, sprays, scalp tattoos and transplants, aimed at giving a healthier-appearing scalp.[4] Grokipedia states dermatologists recommend them as non-invasive complements to minoxidil or surgery for some women with androgenetic alopecia.[1]
A 2022 report described a case of alopecia attributed to hair extensions that was treated with hair transplantation.[8]

A looksmax.org thread asks whether men can wear hair systems convincingly. The original poster says he might get close to ascension by restoring a Norwood 1 hairline, and asks whether the system is obvious to the touch and whether a partner would accept it. One reply says hookups are easy but that a long-term partner would need to be told, and another comments on the stigma attached to toupees.[5] A Lemmy post from a user choosing between wigs and Kanekalon extensions mentions concerns about washing synthetic hair.[9]

Wikipedia reports hair loss along the front hairline or above the ears from prolonged wear, linked to traction alopecia that can become permanent with tight braiding, and glue linked to headaches, bald spots and dermatitis. It mentions patch testing.[2] A dermatology review says the risk of traction alopecia rises with the extent of pulling and duration of traction, and lists extension and weave attachment among the higher-risk styles; in later stages it can progress to irreversible scarring alopecia if traumatic styling continues.[6]
A 2025 review of contact sensitization found synthetic hair extensions can cause contact dermatitis through allergenic components such as acrylates and disperse dyes.[7]

No studies found on artificial hair integrations as a product category for appearance outcomes. Related literature includes reviews of hair camouflage,[4] traction alopecia[6] and contact sensitization to synthetic hair,[7] and a case report of extension-related alopecia treated by transplant.[8]
